title: Maritime Psychology: Definition, Scope and Conceptualization

findings.antecedent: Larger ships, greater mechanization, and reduced manning levels
findings.consequent: Fewer outlets for affiliation, reduced sense of collective identity, individual worth, and support for seafarers
findings.quote: With larger ships, greater mechanization and reduced manning levels, more is required from seafarers and there are fewer outlets for the sort of affiliation that sustains both a sense of collective identity and individual worth and support.

findings.antecedent: Fundamentally unfair and exploitive working environment (e.g., 'sweat ships', flag-of-convenience)
findings.consequent: Counterproductive individual psychological interventions, maintenance of unjust workplaces, negative impact on psychological well-being and rights of individuals, negative impact on sense of organizational justice and expectations for decency
findings.quote: So no matter what sort of clever individual psychological interventions maritime psychologists can develop, implementing these in a fundamentally unfair and exploitive working environment can be counterproductive, individualizing a systems problem (McVeigh et al. 2016).

findings.antecedent: Resolutions adopted by the International Labour Conference (94th maritime session, 2006) concerning 'human element' and 'recruitment and retention of seafarers'
findings.consequent: Increased recognition of psychosocial factors and impetus for further development of maritime psychology
findings.quote: Resolutions adopted by the International Labour Conference at its 94th (maritime) Session in 2006 include a “Resolution concerning addressing the human element through international cooperation between United Nations specialised agencies” (p. X).

findings.antecedent: Many psychologists employed in aviation and space sectors
findings.consequent: Few psychologists employed in the maritime sector
findings.quote: Bengt Schager—who describes himself as a “maritime psychologist”—arguing for the role of psychologists in the maritime transport sector, notes that while many psychologists are employed in the aviation and space sectors, few are employed in the maritime sector (www.profilschager.com).

findings.antecedent: Taking thousands of passengers on a cruise for weeks with a much larger crew
findings.consequent: Requires important leadership and participation skills (more than crewing a Boeing 747 for a few hours)
findings.quote: He points out that while crewing a Boeing 747 across the Atlantic requires many important leadership and participation skills for a few hours, taking thousands of passengers on a cruise for weeks, with a much larger crew, undoubtedly requires these and additional skills.

findings.antecedent: Alert! series ('The International Maritime Human Element Bulletin')
findings.consequent: Helped bring psychological thinking to a wider audience of seafarers
findings.quote: The very useful and accessible Alert! series, subtitled “The International Maritime Human Element Bulletin”, and published by the Nautical Institute, has certainly helped to bring psychological thinking to a wider audience of seafarers.

findings.antecedent: Psychological factors
findings.consequent: Clear importance in a range of issues covered by 'Textbook of Maritime Medicine' (e.g., work roles, manning, piracy, crisis interventions, environmental health, motion sickness, shipwreck, fatigue)
findings.quote: The scope of maritime psychology also overlaps with some complementary fields, so for instance, the “Textbook of Maritime Medicine”, now in its second edition (Carter and Schreiner 2013), is freely available to download. It covers a range of issues where psychological factors are of clear importance.

findings.antecedent: Unfair working conditions (e.g., long hours, lack of leisure/privacy, low-income crew)
findings.consequent: Negative impact on psychological well-being
findings.quote: However, maritime psychology should also be about setting fair working conditions that recognize the needs of seafarers to have leisure time, privacy, opportunities to socialize and indeed sufficient time off work—just as the quote from Sampson illustrates.

findings.antecedent: Diminishing communal living space on board merchant ships
findings.consequent: Reflects legislative environment and company attitude towards social spaces; impacts teamwork and congeniality
findings.quote: For instance, the space allocated to communal living on board merchant ships has been diminishing in recent times (Sampson 2015): the design of living space on board will reflect the legislative environment and the attitude of the company towards social spaces; the use of such space will reflect the sense of teamwork and congeniality on board—and the existence of such an atmosphere will in turn reflect the demand for such space to be built into ships at the design stage.

findings.antecedent: 'Under-considered' welfare of seafarers by many companies
findings.consequent: Low standards for living conditions (despite MLC stipulations)
findings.quote: Sampson and Ellis (2015) argue that the welfare of seafarers is “under-considered” by many companies. While the Maritime Labour Convention (MLC) makes important stipulations regarding seafarer living conditions, these are in reality quite low standards and the aim should be to improve on these rather than simply adhere to them.

findings.antecedent: Modelling human behaviour under extreme stress during ship evacuation
findings.consequent: Very complex and difficult to predict behaviour
findings.quote: Modelling human behaviour under situations of extreme stress is very complex, and such behaviour may be difficult to predict...

findings.antecedent: Minimizing bottlenecks in ship layout (e.g., door sizes, number of doors, heel/trim angles)
findings.consequent: Can guide naval architects to reduce evacuation time
findings.quote: Yuan et al. (2014) illustrate, using a neighbourhood particle swarm optimization model, how door sizes, the number of doors, the number of passengers, along with the ship’s heel and trim angles, all affect the evacuation time of a given ship design.

findings.antecedent: Frailty or mobility of passengers, cognitive or sensory impairments (especially elderly on cruise ships)
findings.consequent: More complex and longer evacuation scenarios and times
findings.quote: What these models may not adequately consider is the frailty or mobility of passengers, the range of cognitive or sensory impairments they may have, and so on. With the majority of passengers on some cruise ships being elderly, it seems likely that the evacuation scenarios and times for these passengers are going to be more complex and take longer than for younger or less impaired passengers.

findings.antecedent: Seafarers attacked or held hostage by pirates
findings.consequent: Concerns about returning to work, sleep disturbances, diminished energy, increased alcohol use, loss of pleasure, irritability, thoughts of suicide
findings.quote: A study of 25 seafarers attacked or held hostage by pirates (Stevenson 2012), which found that most had concerns about returning to work (20), sleep disturbances (12) and diminished energy (10). Some of them also reported increased use of alcohol (7), loss of pleasure from what had been formerly pleasurable activities (6), with fewer reporting a deterioration of significant relationships (5), irritability (5) and sometimes thoughts of suicide (3).

findings.antecedent: Longer time seafarers were held captive
findings.consequent: More severe psychological symptoms
findings.quote: Within this small sample there was no relationship between subjective descriptions of stress, and age, rank or length of service at sea, but there was a relationship with the length of time seafarers were held captive—the longer they were held, the more severe the symptoms.

findings.antecedent: Fear of losing jobs or not being rehired (due to stigma of mental health problems)
findings.consequent: Discourages seafarers from seeking consultation or effective therapy
findings.quote: Stigma discourages many seafarers from seeking consultation or effective therapy … because they fear losing their jobs or not being rehired” (p. 993).

findings.antecedent: Captivity by pirates
findings.consequent: Psychologically equivalent to other serious life-threatening events (terrorist incidents, natural disasters), feelings of detachment/alienation, startled by noises, nightmares, sleep disturbance, anxiety, depressive reactions
findings.quote: They compare the impact of such captivity as being psychologically equivalent to other serious life-threatening events such as terrorist incidents and natural disasters. Participants reported feelings of detachment and alienation from those close to them, being startled by noises, having nightmares and sleep disturbance. Anxiety manifest through apprehension, tension and fear in particular situations, and depressive reactions manifest through low mood, lack of interest and engagement in activities were also noted.

findings.antecedent: Certain styles of command (more democratic)
findings.consequent: Better seafarer well-being
findings.quote: O’Shea (2005) has demonstrated that certain styles of command—generally more democratic styles—are associated with better seafarer well-being.

findings.antecedent: Work Improvement on Board (WIB) programmes (participatory action-oriented training)
findings.consequent: Beneficial, especially when applied flexibly
findings.quote: Researching the effects of Work Improvement on Board (WIB) programmes in the Japanese fishing fleet, Shuji and Kazutaka (2015), using participatory action-orientated training, found such interventions to be beneficial, especially when applied in a flexible manner.

findings.antecedent: Modern merchant ships crewed by seafarers from a range of nationalities
findings.consequent: Important to take account of differences in affiliative preferences, risk perception, and ideas about health and well-being
findings.quote: With modern merchant ships often crewed by seafarers from a range of nationalities, it is important to take account of differences in matters such as affiliative preferences, risk perception and ideas about health and well-being (MacLachlan 2006).

findings.antecedent: Cultivating pluralism (diversity of views)
findings.consequent: Can help solve problems, does not need to be a challenge to a narrow ethos
findings.quote: Organizational culture should also cultivate pluralism (MacLachlan and O’Connell 2000) as a diversity of views in the workplace can in fact help solve problems and does not need to be a challenge to one narrow prevailing ethos (Cox and Blake 1991).

findings.antecedent: High Psychological Capital (PsyCap)
findings.consequent: Positively associated with perceptions of safety climate
findings.quote: Their first study found that PsyCap was positively associated with perceptions of safety climate and importantly this effect still held after controlling for socially desirable responding.

findings.antecedent: High Psychological Capital (PsyCap)
findings.consequent: Perception of safer ship, mediated by job satisfaction
findings.quote: In a second study they demonstrated that PsyCap’s relationship to safety climate was mediated by its association with job satisfaction. While correlational studies cannot determine causality, this nonetheless suggests that those with high scores on psychological capital felt their ship was safer, at least in part, due to them also having greater job satisfaction.

findings.antecedent: Psychological Capital (PsyCap)
findings.consequent: Associated with benefits for some groups (European crew), but not all (Filipino crew)
findings.quote: However, as evidence of the complexity of such a relationship, and the importance of cultural differences in health and performance noted above, this indirect effect was evidenced only for European and not for Filipino crew.

findings.antecedent: Cultivating pluralism (recognizing human differences, finding value in diversity)
findings.consequent: Essence of cultivating pluralism
findings.quote: Taking into account human differences and finding value and benefits in this diversity is perhaps the essence of cultivating pluralism (MacLachlan and O’Connell 2000).

findings.antecedent: Workplace also home for seafarers
findings.consequent: Maritime health focus on occupational health services and international health problems
findings.quote: The fact that the workplace is also the home of seafarers has meant that a considerable focus of maritime has been through the development of occupational health services, with a particular interest in international health problems.

findings.antecedent: Review of International Maritime Health journal publications (2000-2010)
findings.consequent: Identified six themes: healthcare access, tele-health, non-communicable diseases, communicable diseases, psychological functioning/health, safety-related issues
findings.quote: We reviewed publications in the International Maritime Health journal from 2000 to 2010 (MacLachlan et al. 2012) and identified six themes: (1) healthcare access, delivery and integration; (2) tele-health; (3) non-communicable diseases and physical health problems; (4) communicable diseases; (5) psychological functioning and health; and (6) safety-related issues.

findings.antecedent: Strengthening links between international occupational health in maritime and global health
findings.consequent: May contribute to stronger discipline of global occupational health
findings.quote: Indeed strengthening the links between international occupational health in the maritime and global health may contribute to the development of a stronger discipline of global occupational health, concerned with the possibilities for and also the threats of global corporations influencing healthcare across vastly different settings and conditions globally.

findings.antecedent: Gregory and Shanahan’s (2010) 'The Human Element' publication
findings.consequent: Landmark publication, promoted wide dissemination, spurred research questions for satisfying, efficient, and safe seafaring
findings.quote: In this volume we build on previous work in the area and in this regard special mention should be given to Gregory and Shanahan’s (2010) “The Human Element”, which was a landmark publication for the maritime transport industry.

findings.antecedent: Accidents at sea (2000-2005)
findings.consequent: 18 ships collided/sank/grounded/caught fire/exploded daily, 2 sunk daily, average cost $4 million US$ daily, countless human lives. Mostly due to human error.
findings.quote: they note that between 2000 and 2005, on average, every day, 18 ships collided, sank, grounded, caught fire or exploded, resulting in an average of two of them actually sinking each day. The cause of these accidents is mostly due to human error. Such accidents cost an average of around 4 million US$ every day and countless human lives.

findings.antecedent: Positive psychology interventions (general)
findings.consequent: Relatively modest or small-scale positive effects on well-being and performance across work environments
findings.quote: McVeigh et al. provide examples of positive psychology interventions in general, but also such interventions as used in other work contexts. Generally, these studies indicate that relatively modest, or even small-scale, interventions can have quite positive effects, often on well-being and performance, across a range of work environments.

findings.antecedent: Greater personal resilience
findings.consequent: Can act as a buffer to stress
findings.quote: Positive psychology is associated with the idea of hardiness and resilience and there is certainly evidence suggesting that greater personal resilience can act as a buffer to stress (Doyle et al. 2015).

findings.antecedent: Interventions focusing *only* on individual resilience, ignoring broader work context (unjust/stressful situations)
findings.consequent: Problematic, unethical, likely to cause frustration and disengagement
findings.quote: However, McVeigh et al. (2016) have stressed that such interventions that focus only on the resilience of individuals, while ignoring the broader work context in which those individuals are expected to perform, is not only problematic, but also unethical and likely to cause frustration and disengagement.

findings.antecedent: Transferring learning across 'safety critical industries' (Hudson's et al. (2004) levels of safety)
findings.consequent: Maritime industry is somewhat behind aviation, making transfer important
findings.quote: While the aviation industry is probably the best-practice example in safety critical industries, Liston et al. argue that the maritime industry is somewhat behind it, and therefore the transfer of this learning and ethos is important.

findings.antecedent: Aviation sector approach to safety
findings.consequent: Sees different components of safety, quality, health as an inter-connected 'socio-technical system' involving people and technology
findings.quote: One feature that characterizes the aviation sector approach is seeing the different components of safety, quality and health operating as an inter-connected “socio-technical system”; that is, it involves people just as much as it involves technology.

findings.antecedent: Cockpit Resource Management (CRM)
findings.consequent: Crucial part of aviation safety, with Bridge Resource Management (BRM) as maritime equivalent
findings.quote: Cockpit Resource Management is a crucial part of this in the aviation sector, with Bridge Resource Management being its equivalent in the maritime sector.

findings.antecedent: Combining perspectives on designing living and working spaces at sea with perspectives on living and working behaviour at sea
findings.consequent: Potential benefit for ship architecture and design
findings.quote: The chapter illustrates the potential benefit of combining perspectives on designing living and working spaces at sea with per spectives on living and working behaviour at sea.

findings.antecedent: Physical environment (ship architecture)
findings.consequent: Dramatically influences sleep quality, fatigue, opportunities for privacy, attitudes to safety, crew turnover
findings.quote: The physical environment also dramatically influences sleep quality, fatigue and opportunities for privacy; and as such can be expected to influence how people like one ship over another, the extent of crew turnover, but perhaps also their attitudes to safety and to caring for one another.

findings.antecedent: Design engineers' thinking styles
findings.consequent: May benefit from developing additional thinking styles (implied: more human-centered)
findings.quote: Interestingly, they also link this to the sort of thinking styles that design engineers generally have and how they may benefit from developing additional thinking styles.

findings.antecedent: Occupational stress in seafarers (transactional perspective)
findings.consequent: Reviewing stress at individual and organizational levels, considering moderators/mediators
findings.quote: Ana Slišković then addresses occupational stress in seafarers. She adopts a transactional perspective, reviewing stress at the individual and organizational level. She also considers important individual and organizational characteristics as moderators or mediators between sources of stress and stress as an outcome.

findings.antecedent: Fatigue
findings.consequent: Common element in marine accidents attributed to human error, impaired cognition, long-term autonomic, immunologic, metabolic changes, chronic diseases
findings.quote: Jørgen Jepsen and colleagues look in depth at fatigue, which may be considered a particular aspect of stress, but is also multifaceted in its own right. They note that fatigue is a common element in marine accidents attributed to human error, which is of course the major reason for such accidents. They review the effects of fatigue, ranging from immediate effects, such as impaired cognition, to longer term autonomic, immunologic and metabolic changes associated with a number of chronic diseases.

findings.antecedent: Current legislation on fatigue
findings.consequent: Questioned efficacy
findings.quote: They question the efficacy of the current legislation on the issues and compliance with it.

findings.antecedent: Preventive interventions (e.g., Fatigue Risk Management Systems - FRMS)
findings.consequent: Called for
findings.quote: They call for preventive interventions such as the individual Fatigue Risk Management Systems (FRMS).

findings.antecedent: Motion sickness
findings.consequent: Symptoms associated with travel (sea, air, land, space, simulators, wide-screen cinemas), reactions to toxins, chemotherapy, post-operative recovery
findings.quote: Many will be familiar with the association of the symptoms of motion sickness with travel by sea, air and land. Fewer will be aware of the presence of the same symptoms in space travel, in simulators, or with wide-screen cinemas; of the ability to induce such symptoms in the laboratory, without the need for motion; and their presence in reactions to toxins, chemotherapy and post-operative recovery.

findings.antecedent: Motion sickness
findings.consequent: Problematic for maritime work/leisure, potentially fatal in survival situations (loss of bodily fluids, inability to think clearly)
findings.quote: Motion sickness is certainly problematic for maritime work and indeed maritime leisure, but it can also be fatal in survival situations, where the loss of bodily fluids and inability to think clearly can result in loss of life.

findings.antecedent: Effective risk communication
findings.consequent: Requires considering how people pay attention, focus, elaborate on risk factors and protective behaviours
findings.quote: They use the elaboration likelihood model as a framework, where the focus is on how to get people to pay attention to, to focus on—or to elaborate on—certain risk factors and useful protective behaviours.

findings.antecedent: Deeper encoding of information
findings.consequent: More influential, especially in crisis moments
findings.quote: The more deeply people encode information, then the more influential that information is likely to be for them, especially in crisis moments when new information is treated more superficially.

findings.antecedent: Credible, familiar, and liked source of information
findings.consequent: Important for risk communication in shipping
findings.quote: They particularly note the importance of a credible source to provide information, and a source that is familiar and liked. In the context of shipping this of course relates to the value of established relationships between a crew who know and respect each other, something which has diminished in some models of crew management for shipping firms.

findings.antecedent: Mariner cadets completing shore-based training
findings.consequent: Many find being at sea is not something they can manage
findings.quote: This research is important because, at least anecdotally, there are many cases of mariner cadets who complete the shore-based part of their training, only to find that being at sea is not something they can manage.

findings.antecedent: Psychometric instrument (MMPI)
findings.consequent: Offers only one perspective, needs to be part of a pattern of different information from different sources
findings.quote: Rather, any psychometric instrument offers only one perspective in what needs to be a pattern of different types of information, coming from different sources, and collectively pointing to certain conclusions.

findings.antecedent: Sailing as an intervention
findings.consequent: Can promote self-development and be used as therapy
findings.quote: In the final chapter I step outside the confines of maritime transport per se to consider other ways in which maritime psychology may be beneficially developed, focusing on two ways in which sailing can be used as an intervention. First, as an intervention to promote self-development and second sailing as therapy—chiming with the idea of taking therapy outside (Jordan 2013).
